claims.text: The initially single-phase high-entropy alloy has a uniform elemental distribution.
The initially single-phase high-entropy alloy has strong grain-boundary cohesion.
Low-temperature loading with long dwell times can cause stress-assisted, thermally activated segregation of selected alloying elements to grain boundaries.
The segregating elements have lower cohesive energy at the grain boundary.
Elemental enrichment at grain boundaries reduces grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion promotes intergranular decohesion.
Stress and modest thermal activation enhance the kinetic drive for selected elements to segregate to grain boundaries.
The grain-boundary compositional shift can initiate nanoscale embrittling clusters or precipitates.
Segregation and associated loss of cohesion can shift fracture behavior from ductile to brittle despite the alloy's initially single-phase character.
The proposed mechanism is distinct from preexisting impurity- or precipitation-induced grain-boundary embrittlement in conventional alloys.
After low-temperature loading and dwell, grain boundaries will contain higher concentrations of specific alloying elements than in the baseline material.
After the intervention, fracture toughness or impact energy will be lower than in the as-processed baseline.
After the intervention, nanoscale segregated regions or incipient precipitates will be detectable at grain boundaries.
The as-processed alloy has high toughness and ductility because of its uniform composition and strong grain-boundary bonding.
The proposed mechanism is most relevant under low-temperature, prolonged mechanical-stress exposure.
At higher temperatures, dynamic recovery or other mechanisms may dominate over the proposed segregation mechanism.
At very high strain rates, insufficient time is available for significant segregation.
